Milieu.title: Time Lines II
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
As I've written here in recent releases, numbers always play a very significant part in my work, and especially within procedural work where they can be used as sources of rhythmic change, probability, modulation, octaval ranges and so on. 2024 has already seen numerically significant releases issued very close to one another - Vibra 82 being a reference to the birth of my wife, Vibra 83 referring to my own birthdate - and now, Vibra 88 as well, which could only ever be one thing in this series: A study of the powerful Doepfer A-188 "bucket brigade delay" module.
I've explained the way the Doepfer A-188 works before, but in short, it is an analog Karplus-Strong machine, and it exists in no less than seven variations - my modular system contains two different models - which are all different based on their delay stages. Eventually, I would like to have all seven variations in my system, but time and space are in fact finite, especially in the modular synthesis world.
For this second session, itself a duality of two different parts, I've put together a convoluted set of dualities. First, the voice you hear is the summation of two different A-188s - one 256 stage machine and one 1024 stage machine - tuned together in unison, or near-unison, allowing for some beautifully subtle natural chorus to happen between them. Secondly, pun intended, I have used two different scale systems in the quantization of each machine - the first plays a Mixolydian scale in F-sharp, the second plays a Dorian scale in B - and these combine in interesting overlaps that may not necessarily happen were both of the machines playing the same scale in the same key. The whole thing is modulated in unpredictable ways by Buchla's 266t - the "Source of Uncertainty" - and colored by the usage of two different granular resamplers, a four-head tape delay and a deep digital reverberator.
As per the series' usual, more "Time Lines" sessions exist and will follow when their...time...is right.

Milieu.title: Time Lines III
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
"Time Lines III" continues the diverse lineage of my deep love affair with Doepfer's A-188 module line, punctuating itself purposefully with this third entry exploring one of my first sessions with three different A-188 machines. The A-188s are unique synthesizers, with seven distinct variations between them, and I now happily possess three in my modular setup. Their differences are based on the amount of delay stages involved in their circuit design - the larger the number, the more delays - and for a machine that revolves centrally around feedback, these differences are more profound than they may otherwise appear. My modular system has now integrated the 256 stage unit, the 512 stage unit and the 1024 stage unit, and these three are what you hear on this release, each responsible only for a single note.
Using a sequencer called Piconacci in the Allen Synthesis EuroPi module (an open platform machine that runs Python coded applications on Raspberry Pi), I've sent three of the EuroPi's six outputs to each of the A-188s, with Piconacci sending these triggers at time divisions of the master clock signal based on the Fibonacci sequence - the Golden Ratio. In this composition's case, the three divisions are 21, 34 and 55.
From here, each of the A-188 modules play only one note that I've tuned by ear, and three different takes were recorded of the patch. All three takes were layered over one another in FL Studio, with some relatively minor post-processing for filtering and very subtle chorusing (incidentally also based on the BBD circuits in the 188s).
The resultant audio showed up in my wave editor with observable Golden Ratio shaping, which really struck me, understanding just how melodic something rigidly mathematic can truly be. I reserved this session for publication in a special spot in the catalog, because it felt so profound when it was completed. At position number 98, the next to last entry before the milemarker of 100, which is a much larger singular work because of that milestone, "Time Lines III" is in many ways the summation of so many of my ideas that have been explored and published here in the last four years.

Milieu.title: Time Lines IV
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
The fourth iteration of "Time Lines" appears during a snowy Autumn season, or at least it was intended to before being delayed by a change of residence. The ever-flexible Doepfer A-188 units feature here (two of them, and my notes don't include the stage numbers) and are sequenced in the major sixth scale by Carpeggio (in the Phazerville firmware for Ornament & Crime) and Harrington 1200 (in the standard firmware for Ornament). From there, Mutable Instruments' Clouds was employed for a bit of granular reverb and buffer-jittering (which I find pairs very well with the plink-plonk of Karplus sounds when the tempo is right) and Noise Engineering's Versio (running the excellent Multi Versio third-party firmware) handled the stereo delay work. In post, the recording was filtered via an Arturia low-pass and delay-fugued across four different repeating channels, each one inverting the stereo signal and pitch modulating it just a little more, until the fourth channel was the most bent and filtered out.
What all of this amounts to is a pointillist landscape of wide stereo sound, with many small melodic events colliding pleasantly into and off of one another, some of them higher in octaval range than others, engaging the granular reverb tails in different ways. It reminds me a little of Autechre - their palette from the earlier days of Incunabula and Amber, but with their more off-gridded sequencing and serialized presentation in their modern work. It's cheerier than Autechre tend to get, and I'm not sure what that says about me or about this piece, but I think the sounds offered here are pleasant and stimulating - perhaps not for sleeping or meditating, as many of the Vibra sessions often are, but rather for room-coloration or for other daytime ambience needs, like listening at work or while you yourself are engaging in a creative act.
How you use these recordings is always completely up to you, and those usages are, I'm always fond of saying, complete and correct. I hope you find something enjoyable in this surrealistic digital rainfall, and thanks for listening to begin with.

Milieu.title: Watermark
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
'Watermark' is the first session of several focusing on sinewaves that are the result of self-oscillation in filters and phasers. These voices, being sound-shaping utilities rather than true synthesizer voices, behave differently than other "proper" voices, namely in the way they track pitch accurately from a sequencer. This means they are largely unreliable as tuned voices, but modular synthesis rewards curiosity, and in this way, self-oscillating filters can turn something as simple and predictable as a major pentatonic scale into something more exotic that still somehow manages to "make sense" melodically with itself.
This first session explores the "voice" of Stairs, a stereo "Moog-style" ladder filter built by After Later Audio, which includes dedicated outputs for no less than two different slopes of low-pass, a band-pass and a high-pass, along with individual modulation control of both filters and a bias control, which essentially starves the module in the amplifier path in order to elicit unique timbral behaviors from an otherwise standard filter type. Here, you will hear Stairs playing two different major pentatonic scales, sequenced by Ornament & Crime in Quantermain mode, with two of the low-pass outputs becoming a woven pad sound through a four-head tape delay system, and the remaining outputs being processed pointillistically through a Buchla Quad Lo Pass Gate, receiving timing information from a Gate Phaser program in Allen Synthesis' EuroPi module, developed with the compositional approach of Steve Reich in mind.
Altogether, this session resembles a previous Milieu recording a little bit - "Utaru Greenshine Caravan" - mostly due to the pointillism of very small pockets of melodic sound that build a halftone landscape around the listener, but the pad chords beneath these events pass by like a lazy river, recalling instead things like "Recurrent Irrigation" and "Leaden Monarch" - both notably sourced from Moog machines.

Milieu.title: Watermark II
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
The second Watermark session descends from droplets of lake air, with two blue filters self-oscillating into soft sinewaves, playing half-asleep through the harmonic major scale. Occasionally, the notes are truncated when their timing events overlap or collide with one another, while at other times they seem to stretch onward forever. Beneath everything, a soft current of processed brown noise, generated by GoldWave and further shaped by granular processors and delays, widening the spatial mix even more. As the sound that you hear has primarily been produced with a single stereo low-pass analog filter, Watermark sessions once again illustrate just how much music can be derived from simple utilities in the modular environment.
Watermark II is a piece of humid night music, something that evokes the feeling of standing at the edge of the water long after the sun has set, marveling at all the gently undulating darkness. In some respects, Watermark II is just as much about the space between notes as it is about the notes themselves, and it always feels satisfying to find a sensation like this in my otherwise robotic sequencers and clocks - here, time feels syrupy and tired, yielding itself to the lazy melodies that float through it.

Milieu.title: White Alice I + II
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
WHITE ALICE is a new session header for this series, and debuts with a double-album set of the first two Vibra sessions undertaken with the Roland Juno 106 - an iconic and immensely versatile digital polysynth, with an analog filter.
Before discussing the session and its approach, I feel it is relevant to first explain that the Juno is here in the White Pillar Workshop only because a close friend insisted upon giving it to me unexpectedly after we met up for coffee this past Summer. The finer details of why my friend did this are not something I fully know, but part of my reckoning with this unbelievable act of kindness is in how I'm using it in the studio.
Here, on these WHITE ALICE sessions, you can hear what is a deliberately careful hand, shaping the Juno only where and when I felt it necessary, and allowing the machine to breathe and express itself wherever possible. The Vibratelepathic series is designed with these types of approaches in mind, so the Juno is already well-suited to this thinking. It is truly one of the most versatile and beautiful sounding machines I've ever had the pleasure to play, and certainly one that I never thought I'd own. During these sessions, I tend to focus on reactionary decisions rather than fundamental changes, allowing pieces to flow between sections naturally, as a river might meander through different elevation levels and terrain. In this way, the Juno absolutely guides itself. It sounds and feels so certain of its path that I get a very deep sensation of the music making itself.
On a technical level, what you hear on the WHITE ALICE recordings is nothing more than the Juno 106, sequenced via the Arturia Keystep Pro, routed in stereo into my R-EW Audioholistics modular system and navigated in realtime via the assembled ecosystem of modulation and signal processing.
Listening to these sessions now, months later, and considering everything about them, I am convinced of the Juno asserting itself in both physical and philosophical splendor in my studio. Everything about it is emotive and distinct, bringing a surreal, unspoken familiarity with it that recalls past lives, displaced from home, exploring the natural world, getting a glimpse of a mountain top from some distance away, and suddenly knowing where you are, assured in your path, returning to the small village in the ravine that calls your name.
WHITE ALICE, now and forever, in all variations, is for R.G.

Milieu.title: White Alice IV
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
The fourth White Alice session with the Roland Juno 106 polyphonic synthesizer was recorded on the evening of August 5th, 2021 - just over a year ago, as of this publication - and it seems to resume directly from where the drifty White Alice III left off. In the time since White Alice III, there has also been a triple-album set of Variations, issued adjacent to the Vibra catalog (see MMD062:  milieumusic.bandcamp.com/album/white-alice-variations  ), which focused more on various methods of digital/tape degradation in order to 'weather' the otherwise pristine clarity of the Juno, and in this sense, White Alice IV takes aspects of that process into account here also.
Session IV uses a hand-played sequence of chords and melodious lead lines as a looping base, facilitated via the Arturia Keystep Pro, and from there the passages are slowly accumulated upon themselves via the R-EW Audioholistics system, which utilized probabilistic granular samplers and multi-head delay devices to create a pleasantly disorienting fugue-like landscape. Perhaps, a little less moody than White Alice III, session IV feels brighter, hopeful and optimistic, and this feeling is something I would like to focus on with the publication of White Alice IV. White Alice has been lost at sea for some time now, and here, it returns to the continent, a bit more world-weary, but happy to come back home to this sun-kissed valley.

Milieu.title: White Alice VI
Milieu.label: Milieu Music Digital
Milieu.about:
The last White Alice session was published as far back as Vibra 72 in 2023 - the fifth iteration of the session header that consisted of the last two recordings made with the Roland Juno 106 polysynth at the White Pillar Workshop. For this, the sixth, the Juno is finally powered on and properly integrated into the new Cleveland studio space, and so it felt apt that a simple loop study would emerge from the day-long session of mixer channel assignment and MIDI routing. Loop studies are deceptive, always first appearing as something incidental, when the sensation of profundity creeps slowly in as repetition takes hold on the simian brain, and an hour later I find myself sitting there staring at the wall and hallucinating all sorts of audio-visual events in the spaces between the notes.
Texturally and melodically, White Alice VI sits somewhere in my mind between something from RDJ's Selected Ambient Works II, Eno's Neroli and perhaps something from Yoshimura or Jochem Paap. The inimitable digital chorus of the Juno works wonders on the simple passage of melody, and very carefully I've augmented the loop with a stereo-panned delay line and a warm and barely-there modulated reverb send in GoldWave. The Juno always has such distinct personality for a machine that it instantly colors the room it is in, and from a practical standpoint in setting up ZOR as a workspace that is both efficient and emotive, it's difficult to imagine the Juno not remaining a front-and-center staple of the roster from this moment on.
I'm at a point in my work where I want my creative space to function not just in a utility sense for productivity, but as a comfortable and inviting place to explore ideas. White Pillar was cold, isolated and bunker-like, with its windowless walls and fluorescent overheads, and by the end of my tenure there I felt less and less attracted to going down there to record anything - instead spending the last three years in the room above it, with a desk in a hardwood-floored room beside two green windows. So it is with this thinking in mind that ZOR has taken shape, with me accepting that not all of my machines will be installed as permanent fixtures, instead focusing on the machines (like the Juno) that insist on being present at all times.
I think having become accustomed to working within the physical limitations of modular synthesis - only having a set amount of space and power to use for the entire setup - is perhaps also what has informed this thinking. Considerations like these are also where having an ongoing series like Vibratelepathos to attend to has been essential, helping me to determine in a deductive and use-case way exactly how ZOR will function as a creative space. Only time and the fruits of my labors will reveal whether or not these considerations have been correct, so I hope that White Alice VI reaches you in the same way it has reached me - a promising glimpse, with only a singular melody, of what the coming months and years may yet yield here in Cleveland.
